findings.title: Denial cache can reintroduce the exact staleness bug this PR is meant to fix
findings.body: The new permission-denial cache (checked at lines 116-121 and populated at line 154) is consulted before the regular permission cache or any DB fallback, and has the same 30s TTL (shortCacheTTL) as the rest of the caches. Once a Check() call for a specific (namespace,user,action,name,parentFolder) combination is denied, every subsequent Check() for that exact resource short-circuits to `Allowed: false` for up to 30 seconds, with no invalidation hook tied to permission grants/role/team changes. If a user is denied access to a resource and is then granted access (e.g. shared a dashboard, added to a team, or the permission write for a just-created resource lands slightly after the first check), the user will continue to be denied for up to 30 seconds even though a fresh DB query would now return 'allowed'. This reproduces, for the negative-cache case, the same 'cannot access what I should now have access to' symptom that this PR is otherwise trying to fix by falling back to the DB on cache misses.

findings.title: userPermDenialCacheKey is vulnerable to key collisions because its fields are joined with '_' without escaping
findings.body: userPermDenialCacheKey concatenates action, name and parent with a plain '_' delimiter: `namespace + ".perm_" + userUID + "_" + action + "_" + name + "_" + parent`. Grafana dashboard/folder UIDs are allowed to contain underscores (UID validation permits [a-zA-Z0-9_-]+), so two different (action, name, parent) triples can produce the identical cache key string (e.g. action='A', name='B_C', parent='D' vs action='A_B', name='C', parent='D' both yield '..._A_B_C_D'). Because every denial-cache entry stores the same value (`true`), a collision causes a denial cached for one resource/action to be incorrectly served as a cached denial for a completely unrelated resource/action belonging to the same user, wrongly blocking access that was never actually evaluated, for up to the cache TTL.

findings.title: New denial-cache test doesn't actually verify the denial-cache short-circuit
findings.body: In TestService_CacheCheck's 'Should deny on explicit cache deny entry' subtest, the comment claims 'Allow access to the dashboard to prove this is not checked', but the permCache entry is set to `map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}` (an explicit false) rather than `true`. Since reading a missing key or an explicit false both yield `false` from a Go map, and `s.store`/`s.permissionStore`/`s.folderStore` are left as the default empty fakeStore (which returns no permissions and no folders without error), the test would still produce `Allowed: false` via the normal fallback path even if the permDenialCache short-circuit were broken or removed entirely. The test therefore provides no real coverage of the new denial-cache behavior it is supposed to validate.

findings.title: Denial-cache hits and permission-cache hits are reported under the same metric labels
findings.body: In Check(), both a denial-cache hit (line 118) and a positive permission-cache hit (around line 132) increment `s.metrics.permissionCacheUsage.WithLabelValues("true", checkReq.Action)`. These are two distinct caches (permDenialCache vs permCache) with different semantics and TT悠L behavior, but the metric conflates them into a single 'cache hit' counter per action. This makes it impossible to measure the effectiveness/behavior of each cache independently from metrics, reducing the observability value that this feature is supposed to add.

findings.title: List() does not get the same freshness fallback as Check(), so newly created/newly granted resources may still be missing from list results
findings.body: Check() was changed so that when the cached permission map doesn't grant the specific requested resource, it falls back to a fresh DB query (fixing the 'can't access what I just created' bug for single-resource checks). List(), however, only distinguishes cache-hit vs cache-miss as a whole (lines 180-192): if `getCachedIdentityPermissions` returns any cached map at all, that stale map is used as-is to build the list, with no mechanism to detect that it is missing a newly created/newly granted item. As a result, a user who creates a dashboard/folder may be able to directly Check() access to it immediately (via the DB fallback), but the item can still be absent from List() results (e.g. folder/dashboard browse views) for up to shortCacheTTL (30s), partially undermining the stated goal of letting creators see resources they just created.

findings.title: Removing the client-side cache entirely for in-proc mode increases per-check overhead
findings.body: The in-proc AccessClient is now constructed with `authzlib.WithCacheClientOption(&NoopCache{})` instead of a real local cache, meaning every single Check/List call from any in-proc caller must always traverse request validation, the in-proc gRPC channel/interceptor, and the server-side cache lookups, instead of being able to short-circuit via a cheap client-side memory lookup as before. For call patterns that issue many repeated/duplicate permission checks in quick succession (e.g. rendering a page that checks access on many individual items), this removes a previously-available fast path and could noticeably increase CPU/allocation overhead, even though the server-side caches still avoid the DB round-trip.
